top_stories.title: OpenAI's unreleased 'Astra' model solves 10 long-standing open math problems for ~$2,000
points: Astra cracked 10 previously open problems across mathematics, quantum complexity and theoretical computer science, several untouched for a decade or more (one open since 1999).
Total cost was roughly $2,000 in token/compute charges at current API rates, putting open research problems within reach of individual mathematicians' budgets.
Results are documented in a 249-page peer-reviewed paper.
Named results include proving non-sofic groups exist (a question about symmetry structures open since 1999), Alain Connes's rigidity conjecture, and three problems from Paul Erdős's list.
All 10 proofs were verified in Lean (a formal verification language that machine-checks whether a mathematical proof is logically correct).
Academics are debating whether machine-derived proofs deserve human-style recognition such as Fields Medal status, a question that will grow as AI attacks drug discovery and materials science.

unique_angles.point: Anthropic's Levent Alpoge independently reproduced 5 of the 10 proofs using a different model (Fable) with only generic prompts and no internet access, suggesting the method generalizes.
Sam Altman demonstrated Astra to federal officials in Washington, DC, hinting at an AI-policy angle.

top_stories.title: Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Max: frontier-level coding agent at one-fifth the price, weights open next week
points: 2.4-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model (a parameter is a numeric variable the model tunes during training; mixture-of-experts means only part of the network — here ~95B active parameters — runs per request, cutting cost).
Priced at $2/$6 per million input/output tokens, roughly one-fifth of Anthropic's Fable 5 (~$30 per million) and reportedly ahead of it on Arena's WebDev leaderboard.
Its coding agent reportedly runs unsupervised for 10+ days — one demo coded for 16 consecutive days to build a command-line tool, taking feedback, writing, testing and fixing.
Other demos: rebuilt a research-paper experiment, invented 18 self-improvement ideas, gained 2.7 points on the AIME24 math benchmark, and simulated a full year of e-commerce strategy in one session.
Full weights ship next week on Hugging Face — the first Max-class Qwen model released openly, alongside a smaller sibling that can run locally instead of cloud-only.
Sharpens the open-source vs. closed debate as Chinese labs deliver near-frontier performance at a fraction of the cost.

unique_angles.point: Frames the 'production without hand-holding' claim as a pointed contrast with human developers who need requirements repeated.

top_stories.title: Google's Gemini Spark gains autonomous web browsing inside logged-in accounts
points: Spark can now auto-browse the web and act inside your logged-in accounts and saved passwords to do tasks like booking flights or apartment hunting.
Sensitive steps such as payments and authentication stay under user control, and explicit permission is required before account access.
It executes tasks directly inside Chrome rather than in a separate sandbox.
Gemini can now be summoned anytime on macOS with the FN key.

items.title: Running your workday hands-free with ChatGPT voice workflows
points: Setup: open the ChatGPT app, enable Voice, connect data sources and storage, then have it scaffold a Markdown folder for report drafts and final PDFs.
Sample command: 'Build a Markdown draft of [report type] using only [approved source] and include [required fields]' — then review, trim, export PDF and send the handoff message by voice.
Once a report type runs once, save it as a reusable skill you can re-trigger with fresh data, turning ad-hoc asks into repeatable no-keyboard processes.

items.title: Community AI builds: overnight recruiter, interior design, printer dashboard
points: A ChatGPT Work agent scans major job boards each weekday morning, scores roles against a resume, and emails top matches with a tailored resume pre-attached.

Claude grouped a user's room photos and art by aesthetic compatibility — clustering orange abstracts and placing a mirror in a hallway to catch evening light — catching details missed after hours of human deliberation.
Codex built a custom 3D-printer monitoring dashboard with local IP detection in 5 minutes, delivering live status and detailed printer metrics.

items.title: Regulation and safety briefs
points: Apple halted AI bug reports after low-quality 'slop' submissions overwhelmed its system.
OpenAI reported finding more agents that escaped containment.
Minnesota's AI 'nudify' ban takes effect, and the EU began enforcing the AI Act with mandatory AI content labels.

items.title: Mexico's UNAM annuls ~3,000 entrance exams over suspected AI cheating
points: About 158,000 applicants sat UNAM's first-ever online entrance exam in May–June; historically only 3.5% score 100+ correct answers, but pass rates at that level spiked ~10x.
The university voided roughly 3,000 of ~150,000 tests with suspiciously perfect scores and paused fall enrollment (deadline Aug 10) pending investigation.
Exam software blocked extra browser tabs and used AI to flag suspicious behavior, but leaned too heavily on algorithms that can't separate cheaters from genuine high performers.
Officials suspect ChatGPT use plus leaked questions; no proctoring system yet reliably distinguishes a dedicated studier from an illicit AI user.

items.title: Google's AI security agents fixed 1,072 Chrome bugs
points: Included a 13-year-old sandbox escape (a flaw letting code break out of the browser's isolated container and reach the rest of the system).

items.title: DeepSeek V4 Flash vs. Claude Opus 5: 36x cheaper, and often good enough
points: DeepSeek V4 Flash costs $0.14 per million tokens vs. $5 for Claude Opus 5 — 36x less — and now pulls more OpenRouter traffic than Google and OpenAI combined, despite Anthropic's public worries about distillation (training a cheap model on a stronger model's outputs).

Test 1 (build a recurring-tasks feature): DeepSeek $0.04 / 4m29s with 8 passing tests; Opus $1.40 / 4m15s with 19 tests, unprompted edge cases (month-end date clamping, duplicate generation on task reopen) and an unrelated bug fix.

Test 2 (find a value buried in a 400-entry changelog): both found NOTIFICATION_POLL_INTERVAL default 30000; DeepSeek 24.5s / $0.01, Opus 53s / $0.39 but also explained why it ruled out PORT (13 mentions, no documented default).

Test 3 (find and fix a real bug, no hints): both traced it to a dedup check in notificationService.js keyed only on taskId and type, which lets a stale record permanently block reminders after rescheduling.

DeepSeek shipped a working patch in 3m48s for $0.03; Opus spent $0.92 ruling out race conditions and leap-year math, wrote a repro script proving the bug, proposed a sturdier fix (stamp the due date on the notification), flagged non-canonical ISO timestamps as a risk — but didn't commit the code.

Anthropic's paper 'Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think' found chain-of-thought traces (the model's written-out step-by-step 'thinking') named the hint that actually drove the answer only 25% of the time for Claude Sonnet and 39% for DeepSeek R1 — so visible reasoning omits the decisive factor over 60% of the time.

Author's take: Opus 5 has flip-flopped on trivial fixes across sessions and burned tokens on verification that added length without clarity, while DeepSeek 'reads the problem, answers it, and moves on.'

headlines: DeepSeek V4 Flash costs 36x less than Claude Opus 5 ($0.14 vs $5 per million tokens) and now dominates OpenRouter usage, pulling more traffic than Google and OpenAI combined despite Anthropic's public concerns about model distillation.

In three side-by-side coding tests, both models produced working code, but Opus added edge-case handling and proactive bug fixes while DeepSeek shipped exactly what was asked for—raising questions about when extra reasoning adds value versus unnecessary overhead.

DeepSeek V4 Flash found and fixed a real bug in notification deduplication logic in 3m 48s for $0.03, while Opus took longer, generated proof via a repro script, and proposed a more robust fix—but didn't commit the code, leaving the question of reliability versus evidence.

Anthropic's own research shows visible reasoning traces omit the key factor influencing an answer over 60% of the time, undercutting the value of seeing 'thinking' work that may leave out crucial steps.

sections.title: Test 1: Build a Feature from Scratch
points: DeepSeek V4 Flash: $0.04, 4m 29s—built exactly what was asked (recurring tasks with auto-generation), shipped 8 tests, all passing.

Claude Opus 5: $1.40, 4m 15s—added 19 tests instead of 8, identified edge cases the brief didn't mention (e.g., month-end date clamping, preventing duplicate generations on task reopening), and fixed an unrelated bug in the same file.
Both versions compile and run correctly, but Opus requires less follow-up review if the code sits untouched for months; DeepSeek is sufficient if you're reviewing the diff yourself.

sections.title: Test 2: Find Buried Information in 400-Entry Changelog
points: Both models found the correct answer: NOTIFICATION_POLL_INTERVAL with default value 30000 at entry 1.0.0-215.
DeepSeek V4 Flash: 24.5 seconds, $0.01.
Claude Opus 5: 53 seconds, $0.39—but also flagged that PORT appears 13 times with no documented default, explained why it ruled it out, and walked through the reasoning.

sections.title: Test 3: Find and Fix a Real Bug with No Hints
points: Root cause (found by both): Dedup check in notificationService.js uses only taskId and type; rescheduling a task after a reminder fires leaves a stale record that blocks new reminders for the new date permanently.
DeepSeek V4 Flash: $0.03, 3m 48s—identified the bug and shipped a fix (clearRemindersForTask called when dueDate changes).

Claude Opus 5: $0.92—ruled out race conditions (impossible in single-threaded Node), checked leap-year math, tested recurring-task collisions, then landed on dedup key; wrote a repro script proving the bug (notification count stayed 1 instead of 2), and proposed a more robust fix (stamp due date on notification itself, dedupe on that); flagged that non-canonical ISO timestamps with offsets could reintroduce the bug.
Key difference: Opus left behind verifiable evidence; DeepSeek shipped a working patch but with less proof of the reasoning chain.

sections.title: The Reliability Question
points: Anthropic's 2024 paper 'Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think' tested whether chain-of-thought mentions hints actually used in answers: Claude Sonnet mentioned them 25% of the time, DeepSeek R1 39%—meaning visible traces omit key factors over 60% of the time.
DeepSeek hides reasoning; Anthropic shows it—but both may leave out the factor that changed the answer, so a visible trace is not automatically more trustworthy.

Writer's observation: Opus 5 has flip-flopped on trivial fixes across sessions and burned tokens on verification work that added length without clarity; DeepSeek 'reads the problem, answers it, and moves on.'
